key_insight: Interactions with AI agents do more than assist tasks: they alter people’s self-concept and rewire social networks by changing who we trust, how we present ourselves, and how we connect with others. These shifts are measurable and emerge across short- and long-term human–AI engagements.
problem_solved: Addresses the lack of integrated empirical and conceptual understanding of how routine human–AI interactions shape individual identity, interpersonal ties, and broader social structures.
method: Mixed-methods empirical framework combining controlled experiments, longitudinal behavioral tracking, and social-network analysis to detect changes in identity expression and network structure over time.
Surveys and qualitative interviews to capture subjective self-concept shifts alongside objective interaction and graph-based metrics of social ties.
Computational modelling to simulate how individual-level changes aggregate to network-level rewiring and to test intervention scenarios.
impact: Helps AI/ML practitioners anticipate and design for downstream socio-cognitive effects of deployed agents—informing safer personalization, transparency, and social-aware system design. Incorporating these insights can reduce unintended social disruption and improve user wellbeing and adoption.
visual_elements: Sankey diagram showing flow from individual AI interactions → changes in self-concept → shifts in social ties
Before/after social network graphs illustrating network rewiring (nodes colored by identity/attitude)
Timeline or longitudinal plot of key metrics (self-reported identity change, trust, tie strength) across repeated AI interactions
Icon set representing mechanisms (personalization, imitation, feedback loops) with brief callouts
paper_title: Human–AI interactions reshape the self and our social networks
paper_authors: Andreia Sofia Teixeira, Sukhwinder Singh Shergill, Guy Laban
